title: Memory, Addresses and Pointers
summary: Memory is one long row of numbered bytes. A variable is a few of those bytes with a name, its **address** is the number of its first byte, and a **pointer** is a variable whose value is an address.
markdown:
## One long row of bytes Put the last two lessons together. Memory is a row of cells, each cell is one byte, and every byte has a number. That number is the byte's **address**. Addresses are just counting: byte 0, byte 1, byte 2, and so on up to however much memory there is. On a 64-bit system an address is a 64-bit number, and it is always written in hexadecimal, for the reasons the last lesson gave. An address looks like `0x00B3F9A0`. There is nothing more to an address than that. It is the position of a byte in the row. ## Variables are named groups of bytes When you write `int score{ 1200 };` the compiler picks four neighbouring bytes of memory, decides that those bytes are `score`, and puts the bits for 1200 in them. From then on, wherever your code says `score`, the compiled program uses those four bytes. The demonstration below shows five variables and the bytes they occupy. The table lists each variable; the grid underneath is the same memory in address order. ```demo-memory title: Five variables int score = 1200 char grade = 'A' double ratio = 0.75 bool alive = true short lives = 3 ``` Work through these: - Click `score` in the table. Its four bytes light up in the grid. Its address is the address of the **first** of them. - Change `score` to 255, then 256, then 65536. Watch the bytes: 255 fills the first byte, and 256 needs the second. The first byte is the lowest one, which is the little-endian order from the last lesson. - Change `score` to -1. Every byte becomes `FF`. That is two's complement, also from the last lesson. - Change `grade` to `B`. One byte changes, from `41` to `42`. A `char` is a small number that happens to be displayed as a letter. - Look at the bytes of `ratio`. A `double` uses a different scheme, called floating point, so its bytes do not resemble the number at all. The type tells the program how to read them. Everything in a running program is stored this way. A game's health, gold and position are groups of bytes like these, at some address. ## Sizes, alignment and padding The grid has some cells marked `··`. Those are **padding**: bytes that belong to no variable. Processors read a 4-byte value fastest when its address is a multiple of 4, and an 8-byte value when its address is a multiple of 8. This is called **alignment**. To keep every variable aligned, the compiler leaves unused bytes in front of any variable that would otherwise start at an awkward address. Press **Packed tight** in the demonstration to see the same variables with no padding, then switch back. Packing saves a few bytes and makes every read of `ratio` and `lives` slower, which is why compilers do not do it unless told to. The clearest place to see padding from C++ is a `struct`, because the members of a struct are stored in the order you write them. ```cpp #include struct Loose { char grade; // 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding so score is aligned int score; // 4 bytes char rank; // 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding at the end }; struct Tidy { int score; // 4 bytes char grade; // 1 byte char rank; // 1 byte, then 2 bytes of padding at the end }; int main() { std::cout << "Loose: " << sizeof(Loose) << " bytes\n"; std::cout << "Tidy: " << sizeof(Tidy) << " bytes\n"; return 0; } ``` ``` Loose: 12 bytes Tidy: 8 bytes ``` Both structs hold the same three members, six bytes of real data. The order alone makes one of them half as big again as the other. A game with a hundred thousand objects notices that difference. > [!info] Local variables are not promised an order > The demonstration lays variables out in the order they are declared, the way a `struct` does. For ordinary local variables the compiler may choose any order it likes, and an optimising compiler may not store a variable in memory at all, keeping it in a register instead. The rules about size and alignment hold either way. ## Asking where a variable is The `&` operator, placed in front of a variable, gives its address. ```cpp #include int main() { int score{ 1200 }; int lives{ 3 }; std::cout << "score is at " << &score << '\n'; std::cout << "lives is at " << &lives << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` score is at 000000A3D54FF9A4 lives is at 000000A3D54FF9A0 ``` Run it and you will get different numbers from the ones shown here. Run it again and you will probably get different numbers again. That is expected, and the reason is at the end of this lesson. What stays the same is the *distance* between the two addresses. ## Pointers: variables that hold addresses An address is a number, so it can be stored in a variable. A variable that holds an address is called a **pointer**. ```cpp int score{ 1200 }; int* p{ &score }; // p holds the address of score ``` Read `int*` as "address of an int". Two things about `p` matter, and beginners often blur them: | You write | It means | |---|---| | `p` | The address stored in `p` | | `*p` | The `int` that lives at that address | | `&p` | The address of `p` itself, because `p` is a variable and lives somewhere too | Putting `*` in front of a pointer is called **dereferencing** it: go to the address and use what is there. `*p = 50;` does not change `p`. It changes `score`. The demonstration has an array of four `int` values and a pointer `p`. Click a box to aim `p` at it. ```demo-pointers values: 10, 20, 30, 40 ``` Try these, and read the line of C++ and the explanation after each one: - Click `values[2]`. The value of `p` changes to that box's address, and `*p` becomes 30. - Press **\*p += 1**. The number in the box goes up. The array was changed through the pointer, without its name being used. - Type a number next to `*p =` and press **Write**. - Notice that `&p` never changes. `p` is a variable in its own right, with its own address, and only its *contents* change when you aim it somewhere else. ## Moving a pointer Press **p++** in the demonstration and look at the address. It goes up by **4**, not by 1. Adding one to a pointer moves it forward by one *element*, not one byte. An `int` is four bytes, so `p + 1` is the address four bytes further on, which is where the next `int` in an array lives. The compiler does the multiplication for you, using the type the pointer points at. This is called **pointer arithmetic**. An array is nothing more than its elements stored one after another with no gaps, so walking a pointer along it reaches each element in turn. ```cpp #include int main() { int values[4]{ 10, 20, 30, 40 }; int* p{ values }; // an array's name turns into the address of its first element std::cout << *p << '\n'; // 10 ++p; // forward one int, which is 4 bytes std::cout << *p << '\n'; // 20 *p = 99; // write through the pointer std::cout << values[1] << '\n'; // the array changed std::cout << *(p + 2) << '\n'; // two ints further on: values[3] return 0; } ``` ``` 10 20 99 40 ``` In fact `values[i]` is defined by the language to mean `*(values + i)`. Square brackets are pointer arithmetic with a friendlier spelling. ## Addresses you must not use Keep pressing **p++** until `p` goes past the last box. Nothing stops a pointer from holding an address that is outside the array. The pointer is only a number. What you must not do is *dereference* it there. The memory after the array belongs to something else, or to nothing, and reading or writing it is **undefined behaviour**: the program might crash, might quietly damage another variable, or might seem to work until the day it does not. Now press **p = nullptr**, then **\*p += 1**. `nullptr` is the address 0, used by convention to mean "this pointer is not aimed at anything". The operating system makes sure nothing ever lives at address 0, so dereferencing a null pointer stops the program at once with an **access violation**. That is the most common crash in C and C++ programs, and it is the friendly one, because it happens immediately and at the line that is wrong. > [!tip] Give every pointer a value when you create it > A pointer that was never given a value holds whatever bytes happened to be there, which is an address to nowhere in particular. Start every pointer either at a real object or at `nullptr`, and check for `nullptr` before using a pointer that might be empty. ## Where memory comes from A running program's memory is divided into regions with different jobs. You will study each in chapter 2; for now it is enough to know that they exist. | Region | What lives there | How long it lasts | |---|---|---| | **Code** | The program's instructions | The whole run | | **Static data** | Global variables and constants | The whole run | | **Stack** | Local variables of functions that are currently running | Until the function returns | | **Heap** | Memory the program asks for while it runs, with `new` or containers such as `std::vector` | Until the program gives it back | ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Process["One program's memory"] direction TB C["Code
the instructions"] S["Static data
globals and constants"] H["Heap
grows as the program asks for more"] K["Stack
locals of running functions"] end ``` A pointer can hold an address in any of these regions. Much of the skill in low-level programming is knowing which region an address belongs to, and therefore how long it stays valid. ## Why addresses change between runs You saw that `&score` prints a different address each time the program runs. Two things cause that. First, the stack and the heap are handed out by the operating system while the program runs, and what a program gets depends on what happened before. Second, Windows deliberately loads programs at a different place in memory on each run. This is a security feature called **address space layout randomisation**, and chapter 6 explains it. What does not change is the *layout*. Inside a `struct`, `score` is always the same number of bytes from the start. Inside a program, a given global variable is always the same number of bytes from where the program was loaded. So low-level code and debugging tools describe locations as a **base address plus an offset**: find where the thing starts this time, then add a distance that never changes. You will use that idea constantly later in the course. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Confusing `p` with `*p` > `p` is an address. `*p` is the value at that address. `p = 5;` tries to aim the pointer at address 5, which is almost never what was meant. `*p = 5;` stores 5 in the thing it points at. > [!warning] Using a pointer that was never set > An uninitialised pointer holds leftover bytes. Dereferencing it reads or writes some unrelated part of memory. Always initialise pointers. > [!warning] Keeping the address of a local variable after its function returns > A local variable's bytes are reused as soon as the function ends. A pointer to them still holds the old address, but what is there now is something else. This is called a dangling pointer. > [!warning] Going one step too far > An array of four elements has indexes 0 to 3. `values[4]` and `*(p + 4)` are outside it. Off-by-one mistakes with pointers do not produce an error message, only wrong behaviour. > [!warning] Assuming a layout instead of checking it > Padding means the size of a struct is often more than the sum of its members, and members are not always where you would guess. Use `sizeof` and, later in the course, `offsetof` rather than adding up sizes in your head. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the difference between `p`, `*p` and `&p` for a pointer `p`? + `p` is the address held, `*p` the value at that address, `&p` the address of the pointer itself - `p` is the value pointed at, `*p` the address held, `&p` a reference to the value - `p` and `&p` are the same address; `*p` is the value at it - `*p` declares a new pointer, `&p` copies it, `p` is its value > A pointer is a variable too, so it lives somewhere and has its own address, `&p`, which is different from the address it holds. ? Why does adding one to an `int*` move it by four bytes? - Because addresses on x64 always go up in steps of four - Because the compiler rounds every address to a multiple of four - Because one is added to each of the pointer's four bytes + Because pointer arithmetic counts in elements, and an `int` is four bytes > The compiler multiplies by the size of the type pointed at, so `p + 1` is the address of the next `int`. A `char*` plus one moves by one byte. ? What is padding, and why does the compiler add it? - Extra bytes at the end of a program so it fills a whole page + Unused bytes between values or struct members so each value sits at an aligned address - Zeros written over freed memory to hide old values - Spare bytes after an array so it can grow without moving > Keeping each value at an address that is a multiple of its size lets the processor read it fastest. ? Why is dereferencing `nullptr` a crash, and why is that a good thing? + Nothing lives at address 0, so any access is stopped as an access violation and the program fails at the faulty line - Address 0 holds the operating system's code, and crashing protects it from being overwritten - The compiler inserts a check before every dereference, which makes debugging easier > Failing immediately at the bad line is far better than silently corrupting memory. There is no compiler-inserted check: the operating system stops the access. ? Why are memory locations often described as a base plus an offset? - Because pointers can only hold small numbers - Because the CPU cannot read an absolute address directly + Because absolute addresses change between runs, but the distance from a base to a value does not - Because it saves memory compared with storing full addresses > Find the base (the start of a struct or loaded program) at run time and add the fixed offset, and you reach the value every time. ? What is the address of a variable? - The value stored in it + The position in memory of its first byte - The number of bytes it takes up > Memory is a numbered row of bytes. A variable occupies one or more of them, and its address is the number of the first. ? An `int` is at address `0x1000`. `int* p` points at it. What address is `p + 1`? - `0x1001` + `0x1004` - `0x1008` > Adding one to a pointer moves it by one element. An `int` is four bytes, so the next `int` starts four bytes further on. ? After `int score{ 7 }; int* p{ &score }; *p = 20;` what is true? - `p` now holds 20 + `score` is now 20 - `score` is still 7, because only a copy changed > `*p` means "the int that p points at", which is `score` itself. Nothing was copied. `p` still holds the address of `score`. ? A struct has a `char`, then an `int`, then a `char`. Why is `sizeof` 12 and not 6? - Every member is rounded up to 4 bytes + Padding keeps the `int` and the struct size at multiples of 4 - The compiler reserves space for future members > The `int` needs to be aligned, so three unused bytes follow the first `char`. Three more follow the last `char` so that the next struct in an array would also be aligned. ? What happens when a program dereferences a null pointer on Windows? - It reads the value 0 - Nothing, the statement is skipped + Windows stops it with an access violation > Nothing is ever placed at address 0, precisely so that this mistake is caught the moment it happens. ? The same program prints a different address for the same variable each time it runs. Why? - The compiler is rebuilt each time + Windows places the program and its stack differently each run - The variable's value is different each time > Addresses are assigned at run time and Windows randomises them on purpose. The distances between things inside the program stay the same, which is why locations are described as a base plus an offset. ```
ideas:
- In the memory demonstration, set `lives` to 300 and work out its two bytes before you look. 300 is `0x012C`.
- Set `grade` to 97 and see which letter appears. Then try 48.
- In the pointer demonstration, use only **p++** and **\*p += 1** to add one to every element of the array.
- Copy the `Loose` and `Tidy` structs into the Playground and add a `double` member to each. Predict both sizes first, then run it. Try moving the `double` to different positions.
- Run the `&score` example several times in the Playground. Write down the two addresses each time and subtract them. The addresses change; check whether the difference does.

cards.q: What is the difference between `p`, `*p` and `&p` for a pointer `p`?
cards.a:
`p` is the address held, `*p` the value at that address, `&p` the address of the pointer itself

A pointer is a variable too, so it lives somewhere and has its own address, `&p`, which is different from the address it holds.

cards.q: Why does adding one to an `int*` move it by four bytes?
cards.a:
Because pointer arithmetic counts in elements, and an `int` is four bytes

The compiler multiplies by the size of the type pointed at, so `p + 1` is the address of the next `int`. A `char*` plus one moves by one byte.

cards.q: What is padding, and why does the compiler add it?
cards.a:
Unused bytes between values or struct members so each value sits at an aligned address

Keeping each value at an address that is a multiple of its size lets the processor read it fastest.

cards.q: Why is dereferencing `nullptr` a crash, and why is that a good thing?
cards.a:
Nothing lives at address 0, so any access is stopped as an access violation and the program fails at the faulty line

Failing immediately at the bad line is far better than silently corrupting memory. There is no compiler-inserted check: the operating system stops the access.

cards.q: Why are memory locations often described as a base plus an offset?
cards.a:
Because absolute addresses change between runs, but the distance from a base to a value does not

Find the base (the start of a struct or loaded program) at run time and add the fixed offset, and you reach the value every time.

cards.q: What is the address of a variable?
cards.a:
The position in memory of its first byte

Memory is a numbered row of bytes. A variable occupies one or more of them, and its address is the number of the first.

cards.q: An `int` is at address `0x1000`. `int* p` points at it. What address is `p + 1`?
cards.a:
`0x1004`

Adding one to a pointer moves it by one element. An `int` is four bytes, so the next `int` starts four bytes further on.

cards.q: After `int score{ 7 }; int* p{ &score }; *p = 20;` what is true?
cards.a:
`score` is now 20

`*p` means "the int that p points at", which is `score` itself. Nothing was copied. `p` still holds the address of `score`.

cards.q: A struct has a `char`, then an `int`, then a `char`. Why is `sizeof` 12 and not 6?
cards.a:
Padding keeps the `int` and the struct size at multiples of 4

The `int` needs to be aligned, so three unused bytes follow the first `char`. Three more follow the last `char` so that the next struct in an array would also be aligned.

cards.q: What happens when a program dereferences a null pointer on Windows?
cards.a:
Windows stops it with an access violation

Nothing is ever placed at address 0, precisely so that this mistake is caught the moment it happens.

cards.q: The same program prints a different address for the same variable each time it runs. Why?
cards.a:
Windows places the program and its stack differently each run

Addresses are assigned at run time and Windows randomises them on purpose. The distances between things inside the program stay the same, which is why locations are described as a base plus an offset.
